Growth trajectories of Cape horse mackerel (Trachurus capensis) in the southern Benguela upwelling system have been characterised through extensive otolith-based ageing studies. Field surveys indicate that individuals attain a maximum total length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], with the largest specimens typically recorded in deeper, cooler waters off the western Agulhas Bank. Age-at-length keys derived from trawl survey data reveal that this species follows a relatively rapid initial growth phase before approaching its asymptotic size. The length-weight relationship commonly applied for this stock (W = 0.01023 * L^2.94) translates this terminal length into an ultimate wet weight of 1728 g [Wwi = 1728 g], placing adult Trachurus capensis among the larger carangids in the region. Population-level comparisons indicate that growth parameters vary latitudinally, with individuals off Namibia exhibiting slightly lower asymptotic lengths than their South African conspecifics, a pattern potentially linked to differences in prey availability and water temperature. These growth characteristics are essential inputs for the per-recruit models currently used to inform management advice for this commercially important species.

Reproductive development in Trachurus capensis has been investigated through histological analysis of gonadal tissue from monthly research surveys. The total length at which fifty percent of individuals are classified as mature, based on the presence of vitellogenic oocytes or spermatogenic lobules, is 32.5 cm [Lp = 32.5 cm]. The corresponding wet weight at this maturity milestone, derived from the same length-weight conversion used for growth estimation, is approximately 285 g [Wwp = approximately 285 g]. This size at puberty is reached relatively early in the species' lifespan, allowing individuals to participate in spawning events before attaining their full adult dimensions. Macroscopic staging of ovaries further indicates that gonadal condition peaks during the austral spring and summer months, with active spawning concentrated between September and February. The gonadosomatic index (GSI) reaches a mean annual maximum of 5% [GSI = 5%] during this reproductive peak at an ambient water temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C].

The early life stages of Trachurus capensis are characterised by rapid ontogenetic development that begins with the fertilised egg. Based on an average egg diameter of approximately 1 mm, the calculated wet weight of a newly fertilised ovum is 0.000523 g [Wwb = 0.000523 g]. At a typical incubation temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C], eggs complete embryonic development and undergo eclosion after roughly 4.55 days [ab = roughly 4.55 days], yielding a yolk-sac larva that remains in an endotrophic state for a brief period. This brief embryonic phase is followed by the onset of exogenous feeding, marked by mouth opening and the commencement of first prey capture. Larval survival during this critical transition is highly dependent on the availability of suitable zooplankton prey, particularly copepod nauplii and early copepodite stages. The small initial mass of the newly hatched larva underscores the vulnerability of these early life stages to starvation, as endogenous yolk reserves are consumed within a narrow window before the trophic switch must occur.

Longevity estimates for Trachurus capensis have been derived from annulus counts on sagittal otoliths, with the oldest individuals recorded in the commercial bycatch reaching a maximum lifespan of 7300 days [am = 7300 days] at the prevailing temperatures of the southern Benguela, approximately 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. This extended lifespan, equivalent to roughly two decades, positions the Cape horse mackerel as a moderately long-lived pelagic species relative to other small pelagic fish such as sardine or anchovy, which rarely exceed a decade. The species' life-history strategy combines a relatively protracted reproductive lifespan with iteroparous spawning, allowing individuals to buffer against interannual variability in recruitment success. Age-structured stock assessments rely on these longevity estimates to parameterise natural mortality rates and to evaluate the long-term sustainability of current fishing pressure. Senescence in older individuals is inferred from declining condition indices and reduced reproductive output, though direct observations on post-reproductive mortality remain limited.

Comparative studies within the genus Trachurus reveal notable differences in life-history traits that correlate with latitudinal distributions. Reaching a maximum length of 60 cm [Li = 60 cm], Trachurus capensis occupies an intermediate position between the smaller horse mackerel of the North Atlantic and the larger Trachurus murphyi of the South Pacific. The body mass at which reproductive maturation typically commences, 285 g [Wwp = 285 g], is consistent with a temperate carangid that initiates spawning at roughly half its asymptotic body size. The gonadosomatic index reaches a mean annual peak of 5% [GSI = 5%] at 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]. This relatively conservative reproductive strategy may reflect a trade-off prioritising the somatic maintenance necessary to sustain a multi-decadal lifespan of roughly 20 years [am = roughly 20 years], as recorded from otolith annuli at a temperature of 11.2 °C [T = 11.2 °C]analyses. Such life-history characteristics carry direct implications for assessing the species' resilience to commercial exploitation.
